newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ shares dip to softer close, Lion stalks higher.
newsitem.headline: NZ shares dip to softer close, Lion stalks higher.

text.p: * NZ stock market closes easier on moderate volume
* Lion Nathan, up three cents, tops turnover
* Brierley unchanged after Bass oil float
Price movements at close
LAST CHG * NZSE40 cap index -6.43 at 2,507.34

WELLINGTON, Jul 8 (Reuter) New Zealand stocks closed slightly weaker on Tuesday on moderate volumes, and brokers saw the market in sideways drift between main reporting seasons.
The NZSE40 capital index finished down 6.43 points, or 0.26 percent, at 2,507.35 on turnover worth NZ$68.2 million.
BZW broker Philip Hardie-Boys said the market had opened a little better but traded down.

"The volume is not aggressive and given the market has had a good run there is a little bit of readjustment of portfolios going on at the moment with reasonable demand from overseas," he said. "All in all the market seems pretty healthy really."
Brokers said strong overseas demand for share in brewer Lion Nathan lifted the stock two cents to $3.77 and saw it top turnover with 3.4 million shares traded.
"The only thing we have heard is that (rival brewer DB Group's) beer volumes have slipped a little, but that has been forecast anyway," another dealer said.
DB Group closed up one cent at $2.30.
Telecom Corp hit an all-time intraday high of $7.91 before trading back to close off one cent at $7.82.

Brierley Investments closed unchanged after easing a cent in early trade after the A$220 million float of its Australian oil interests, through the Bass Strait Oil Trust, saw shares trading below their A$5 issue price.
Hardie-Boys said PPI, retail sales and CPI data in the U.S. could provide a focus towards the end of the week.

"We are really in the terrible mid-reporting season -- in the U.K. it is holiday season, in the States it is summer and they have just had their fourth of July celebration. It tends to slow down a bit," he said.
"It might go into a bit of a holding pattern unless we see a break in interest rates one way or the other, or in the currency," he added.
